findings.title: An update of orders spends nearly all its time waiting on locks, 28.7 s per run
findings.summary: Of its 2 min in the last 8 h 25 min, 2 min went to waiting for locks other sessions held. That time belongs to the sessions holding the locks: making this statement faster won't help, shortening the transactions that hold the rows will.

fix.summary: Find the holder while it happens (Live shows who blocks whom). Keep the holding transactions short and commit before slow work; make UPDATE and DELETE filter on an index so they lock only the rows they change; touch rows in the same order everywhere.

verify: Re-scan: lock waits should be a small part of its time.

findings.title: A read from order_items times out on every run, at about 15 s
findings.summary: None of its 6 runs in the last 8 h 25 min finished. 6 were cancelled by the client after 15.0 s on average, which is what a command timeout looks like. A run that doesn't finish still costs the time it ran, and the application retries it or shows an error.

fix.summary: Cancelled runs are almost always the application's command timeout (here about 15 s; 30 s is the default in ADO.NET and most drivers). Make the statement faster first: open its plan. If it legitimately runs long, raise the timeout for this call only.

verify: Re-scan after the change: runs that fail or are cancelled should drop to near zero.

findings.title: A read from orders fails 25% of the time
findings.summary: 50 of its 200 runs in the last 8 h 25 min didn't finish. 50 ended in an error. A run that doesn't finish still costs the time it ran, and the application retries it or shows an error.

fix.summary: Query Store counts the errors but doesn't keep them. Capture them for a while with an Extended Events session on error_reported for this database, read the ring buffer, then drop the session.

verify: Re-scan after the change: runs that fail or are cancelled should drop to near zero.

findings.title: A read from orders spends nearly all its time waiting on locks, 23.9 s per run
findings.summary: Of its 1 min in the last 8 h 25 min, 1 min went to waiting for locks other sessions held. That time belongs to the sessions holding the locks: making this statement faster won't help, shortening the transactions that hold the rows will.

fix.summary: Find the holder while it happens (Live shows who blocks whom). Keep the holding transactions short and commit before slow work; make UPDATE and DELETE filter on an index so they lock only the rows they change; touch rows in the same order everywhere.

verify: Re-scan: lock waits should be a small part of its time.

findings.title: An update of wide writes 7.9 KB of transaction log per row it changes
findings.summary: It wrote 232 MB of transaction log in the last 8 h 25 min: 83% of what statements wrote, about 7.9 KB per row it changed. Every byte of transaction log is also written to backups and sent to replicas, so it drives replication lag, backup size and checkpoints.

fix.summary: Log per row this high usually means wide rows rewritten whole, many indexes updated, or one transaction per row. Batch writes into transactions of about a thousand rows, update only the columns that change, and drop indexes nobody reads (see Indexes).

verify: Re-scan: its share of the transaction log and the bytes per row should drop.

findings.title: Sessions wait 37.3 s each on row locks in orders
findings.summary: Since pk_orders was loaded into memory, sessions waited 5 times for locks on its rows and pages, 3 min in all, 37.3 s each on average. Waits like these come from transactions that hold rows for long, or from writes whose filter isn't indexed and so lock more rows than they change.

fix.summary: Keep the transactions that change orders short and commit before slow work; make their WHERE use an index so they lock only the rows they change. If readers are the ones waiting, READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT lets them read the last committed version instead: it changes what readers see and uses tempdb, so test it first.
fix.sql:
-- Readers stop waiting for writers; test first
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;

verify: Re-scan a day later: lock waits on this index should stop growing.
caveats: Counted since the index's metadata was loaded into memory, usually since SQL Server started.

findings.title: Inserts into hot queue for the last page of pk_hot
findings.summary: pk_hot starts with a value that only grows (id), so every insert goes to the same last page. Concurrent inserts wait for each other's latch on it (PAGELATCH_EX): 106K waits, 53.6 s in all since the index was loaded. It gets worse with more concurrent writers.

fix.summary: SQL Server 2019 can pace inserts into a sequential key so the page isn't handed back and forth: turn OPTIMIZE_FOR_SEQUENTIAL_KEY on for this index. It's a metadata change and takes effect at once.

verify: Re-scan under the same load: page latch waits on this index should stop growing.

findings.title: Compiling takes 34% of the time of a read from orders
findings.summary: Each compile takes 23 ms and the statement then runs for 45 ms: 34% of its time goes to compiling, 6.9 s in the last 8 h 25 min (a new plan for every run). Planning gets expensive with many joins, partitions or large statistics targets, and it repeats when the plan isn't reused.

fix.summary: It compiles on every run: look for OPTION (RECOMPILE), a procedure created WITH RECOMPILE, or literal values in the text instead of parameters (sp_executesql with parameters reuses one plan). Forced parameterization reuses plans for statements that differ only in literals, for the whole database: test it first.
fix.sql:
-- Database-wide: statements that differ only in literals share a plan
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET PARAMETERIZATION FORCED;

verify: Re-scan: planning should be a small part of its time.
caveats: Query Store keeps compile time for the query's whole life, so the time is spread over the window's runs.

findings.title: A read from order_items returns 20K rows per run
findings.summary: Each run sends 20K rows to the application; its 25 runs in the last 8 h 25 min moved 500K rows. Few screens or jobs need that many at once: the database reads them, the network carries them and the application holds them in memory.

fix.summary: Return only what's used: page the results (keyset pagination, or LIMIT / OFFSET … FETCH), filter in SQL rather than in the application, select only the columns you need, and aggregate in the database.

verify: Re-scan: rows per run should drop to what a page or a job actually uses.

findings.title: SQL Server doesn't trust 2 constraints on child
findings.summary: fk_child_parent and ck_child_amount were created or re-enabled WITH NOCHECK, so existing rows were never checked against them. The optimizer only relies on trusted constraints: it can't remove a join to the referenced table when no columns from it are used, or rule out values a check constraint excludes, so it plans work it could skip.

fix.summary: Check the existing rows so SQL Server trusts them again. It reads the whole table and locks it while it runs: schedule it off-peak. It fails if a row breaks the constraint; fix those rows first.
fix.sql:
ALTER TABLE [archive].[child] WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT [fk_child_parent];
ALTER TABLE [archive].[child] WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT [ck_child_amount];

verify: Re-scan: the constraint should no longer be listed.

findings.title: An update of orders fails 28% of the time (1205 lock wait timeout)
findings.summary: 12 of its 43 runs since its statistics began 3 h 5 min ago didn't finish. 12 ended in an error; the recent ones were 1205 lock wait timeout. A run that doesn't finish still costs the time it ran, and the application retries it or shows an error.

fix.summary: Another transaction holds the rows it needs for longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout: find the holder in Live while it happens and keep transactions short. The recent errors and their messages are in performance_schema.

verify: Re-scan after the change: runs that fail or are cancelled should drop to near zero.
caveats: MySQL counts errors per statement since it started, so old failures stay in the total until it restarts.

findings.title: MySQL guesses how many orders rows match promo_code and created_at: no histogram
findings.summary: 2 of the heaviest queries filter orders on promo_code and created_at, which no index starts with and no histogram describes, so MySQL assumes a fixed share of rows match (10% for =, a third for ranges); EXPLAIN shows filtered = 10.00%, one of those guesses. When the real share is far off, common for status flags and skewed values, it picks the wrong join order or access path. A histogram costs nothing at query time and changes only when you run ANALYZE again.

fix.summary: Build a histogram for these columns. It reads the table once; MySQL doesn't refresh it on its own, so run it again after large data changes.
fix.sql: ANALYZE TABLE `shop`.`orders` UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON `promo_code`, `created_at` WITH 64 BUCKETS;

verify: Re-scan: the columns should have histograms, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE should show estimated rows close to actual for that filter.
caveats: An index is also suggested for promo_code; once it exists the optimizer estimates from the index instead.

findings.title: A read from orders returns 247K rows (≈ 17.4 MB) per run
findings.summary: Each run sends 247K rows to the application, about 17.4 MB at the plan's estimated 74 B per row; its 214 runs since its statistics began 9 h 1 min ago moved 52.8M rows. Few screens or jobs need that many at once: the database reads them, the network carries them and the application holds them in memory.

fix.summary: Return only what's used: page the results (keyset pagination, or LIMIT / OFFSET … FETCH), filter in SQL rather than in the application, select only the columns you need, and aggregate in the database.

verify: Re-scan: rows per run should drop to what a page or a job actually uses.

findings.title: Planning takes almost all of the time of a read from orders
findings.summary: Each plan takes 90 ms and the statement then runs for 0.05 ms: almost all of its time goes to planning, 27.0 s since its statistics began 9 h 1 min ago (a new plan for every run). Planning gets expensive with many joins, partitions or large statistics targets, and it repeats when the plan isn't reused.

fix.summary: Prepare it once and reuse it: most drivers do when you bind parameters (pgjdbc prepareThreshold, Npgsql Max Auto Prepare, psycopg prepare=True). Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, prepared statements need 1.21+ with max_prepared_statements set. If planning stays slow when reused, look at the number of joins and partitions it touches.

verify: Re-scan: planning should be a small part of its time.

findings.title: JIT compilation takes longer than running a read from products
findings.summary: PostgreSQL compiles parts of this statement to machine code before running it, because the planner estimates its cost above jit_above_cost (100000). That takes 31 ms of its 32 ms per run (3.7 s in all since its statistics began 9 h 1 min ago). JIT pays off for long analytical queries; for a statement that runs in 32 ms the compiling costs more than it saves, usually because the planner overestimates its cost.

fix.summary: Raise the cost threshold so JIT only starts for genuinely long queries, or turn it off for the application's role. Fixing the row estimate that inflates the cost also helps.

verify: Re-scan: JIT time per run should drop to zero or near it, and the average run time with it.

findings.title: An update of wide writes 8.3 KB of WAL per row it changes
findings.summary: It wrote 174 MB of WAL since its statistics began 9 h 1 min ago: 14% of what statements wrote, about 8.3 KB per row it changed. Every byte of WAL is also written to backups and sent to replicas, so it drives replication lag, backup size and checkpoints. About 86% of it is full-page images: the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs the whole 8 KB page.

fix.summary: Touch each page once per checkpoint: batch the changes (one statement for many rows, sorted by key) rather than many scattered single-row writes. Every index on the table adds its own WAL: drop indexes nobody reads (see Indexes). When full-page images dominate, wal_compression shrinks them, and a longer checkpoint interval logs fewer of them.
fix.sql:
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_compression = on;  -- lz4 or zstd on PostgreSQL 15+
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

verify: Re-scan: its share of the WAL and the bytes per row should drop.

findings.title: The inactive replication slot analytics_slot keeps 1.1 GB of WAL
findings.summary: A replication slot keeps every WAL file its consumer hasn't confirmed. analytics_slot is inactive, so the WAL it holds keeps growing until the disk fills and the server stops accepting writes.

fix.summary: If nothing will consume this slot again, drop it. To keep a slot from filling the disk, cap what slots may keep (PostgreSQL 13+).

verify: Re-scan: the lag should be seconds, or the slot gone.

findings.title: The check constraint wide_touched_positive on wide was never validated
findings.summary: wide_touched_positive was added NOT VALID, so rows that existed then were never checked. Until it is validated the planner can't use it to skip the table when a query's filter contradicts it (constraint exclusion).

fix.summary: Validate it: PostgreSQL scans the table but takes only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, so reads and writes continue. It fails if a row breaks the constraint; fix those rows first.
fix.sql: ALTER TABLE archive.wide VALIDATE CONSTRAINT wide_touched_positive;

verify: Re-scan: the constraint should no longer be listed.

findings.title: No update to wide is HOT: each one rewrites every index
findings.summary: An update that changes no indexed column and finds room on the same page is HOT: it writes no index entries and its old version is cleaned up without VACUUM. None of wide's 21K updates were, so each wrote a new entry in both of its indexes. 100% of them moved to another page because their own was full (fillfactor 100).

fix.summary: Leave room on each page so updated rows fit next to the old version: a fillfactor of 85–90 is typical for tables updated often. It applies to pages written from now on; existing pages get the room as rows move (pg_repack rewrites the table online if you want it at once). If an index covers a column that changes on every update (updated_at, status, counters), dropping it makes those updates HOT too.

verify: Re-scan a few days later: the HOT share counts since the last statistics reset, so compare how n_tup_hot_upd grows against n_tup_upd.

findings.title: wide is about 74% empty space (≈ 123 MB)
findings.summary: From its row count and average row width, wide's rows need about 44.0 MB; it takes 167 MB. New rows reuse freed space, but every scan still reads the empty pages, and the cache holds them. This is an estimate from statistics, good to tens of percent; pgstattuple measures it exactly.

fix.summary: Measure it exactly first. To give the space back, rewrite the table: pg_repack does it online; VACUUM FULL does it while blocking all reads and writes. If the table keeps growing, make autovacuum visit it more often so freed space is reused sooner.

verify: Re-scan after the rewrite: the estimate should fall under 20%.
